context:
Archive item 1: Archival Research Notebook
Source format: research notebook

Spent the morning at the National Archives of Singapore (NAS) on Canning Rise. I was looking for the Straits Settlements Birth Registers, but I got distracted by the index to the Malacca Registration District. The index is on microfilm (NAS MICROFILM 6789, reel 2). I found an entry that could be relevant:

- Name: Lim Tian Soo (also spelled “Lim Tian Su” in the index)
- Registration District: Malacca
- Year: 1875
- Volume: 4, Folio: 118

I did not pull the actual register page because the microfilm reader was having focus issues. The index entry is promising but I must see the original page to verify the date of birth and the parents’ names. The index alone is not sufficient for a genealogical citation.

---

**22 January 1990**

Wrote to the National Archives of Malaysia (Arkib Negara Malaysia), Kuala Lumpur, to ask if they hold the Malacca Birth Registers for 1875. I have a standard request letter that I use for such queries. I sent it by registered post. I should expect a response in 4–6 weeks.

Also telephoned Cousin Margaret to ask if she has any other letters from Auntie Siew that mention Uncle Tian. She said she has a small tin box of papers that belonged to her mother (my mother’s other sister, Siew Hiang). She will look through it when she has time. I reminded her that even a scrap of paper with a date would help.

---

**3 February 1990**

Cousin Margaret telephoned. She found a postcard from Auntie Siew to her mother, postmarked 1935, that mentions “Tian Soo’s eldest daughter is getting married in June.” This is not a birth record, but it confirms that Lim Tian Soo had at least one daughter. The family tree in my possession (hand-drawn by my grandfather, circa 1950) lists a daughter named Lim Poh Neo, but gives no dates. I will add a marginal note to the family tree: “Poh Neo, daughter of Tian Soo, married June 1935 (per postcard, Siew to Siew Hiang, 1935).”

Marginalia on the postcard: The postmark is partially illegible, but the year 1935 is clear. The card was posted from Malacca, and the stamp is the 2-cent Straits Settlements issue with a portrait of King George V.

---

In the Archival Research Notebook, Lim Tian Soo birth_year is recorded as 1875. Record status: historical.

**17 February 1990**

Received a reply from Arkib Negara Malaysia. They confirm that they hold the Malacca Birth Registers for the period 1872–1900, but the registers for 1875 are in poor condition. They suggest I write to the Registry of Births and Deaths, Malacca, to request a search. They also note that some registers were damaged during the war, and that the microfilm copies held in Singapore may be the best source.

I have decided to try the Singapore microfilm again, but this time I will use a different reader. The NAS staff said that the focus issue is on the machine, not the film. I will book the machine for a full morning session.

---

**24 February 1990**

Morning at NAS. I booked microfilm reader 3, which is in better condition. I re-loaded reel 2 of MICROFILM 6789 and went to the Malacca Birth Register for 1875. The index entry led me to Volume 4, Folio 118. The page is very faint, but I could make out the following:

- No. of entry: 412
- Name of child: Lim Tian Soo
- Sex: Male
- Date of birth: 17 March 1875
- Place of birth: 8, Jalan Tengkera, Malacca
- Name of father: Lim Cheng Huat (occupation: trader)
- Name of mother: Tan Kim Neo (no occupation listed)
- Informant: Lim Cheng Huat (father), 21 March 1875

This is the registration record. The date of birth is 17 March 1875. The index had only given the year, so this is a new finding. I have transcribed the entry fully into the notebook. I have also made a photocopy of the page (NAS photocopy request no. 1990-0214). I will file the photocopy with the family papers.

I must be careful: the register is a contemporary record, made in 1875, and is therefore a historical source. The birth year of Lim Tian Soo is 1875. This is now a recorded fact in this notebook, based on the register entry. I will not revise this unless I find a conflicting record, which is unlikely because the register is the primary source.

---

**2 March 1990**
I have been thinking about the place of birth. The register says "8, Jalan Tengkera, Malacca." This is a street address. But the family story, as told by my grandmother and recorded in the family Bible, says that Lim Tian Soo was born at Raffles Place. I have never been able to reconcile these two statements. The family Bible entry is in my aunt's handwriting, and she wrote it down in the 1930s, many years after the event. It says: "Lim Tian Soo, born at Raffles Place, in the year 1875." No month or day is given.

I need to be careful here. The register is a contemporary record, made in 1875, and is therefore a historical source. The family Bible is a later record, made in the 1930s, and is therefore not contemporary. However, the family Bible may preserve an oral tradition that is older than the written entry. The question is whether the oral tradition is reliable.

I have decided to investigate the Raffles Place connection further. There are several possibilities:

1. The family moved from Malacca to Singapore when Lim Tian Soo was an infant, and the family Bible entry reflects the place where he grew up, not where he was born.
2. The family had a business address at Raffles Place, and the Bible entry confuses the family residence with the business premises.
3. The Bible entry is simply wrong.

I will need to find evidence that bears on these possibilities. The first step is to establish whether the family had any connection to Raffles Place in the 1870s or 1880s.

---

**16 March 1990**

Spent the afternoon at the National Library, looking at old street directories. I consulted the Singapore and Straits Directory for 1880, 1885, and 1890. These are available on microfilm at the library. The 1880 directory lists a "Lim Cheng Huat, trader" at 12 Raffles Place. The 1885 directory lists the same name at the same address. The 1890 directory does not list Lim Cheng Huat, but it does list a "Lim Tian Soo, clerk" at 7 Raffles Place.

This is a significant finding. The father, Lim Cheng Huat, was at Raffles Place by 1880, which is only five years after the birth of Lim Tian Soo. The son, Lim Tian Soo, is listed at Raffles Place in 1890, when he would have been fifteen years old. This suggests that the family had a long association with Raffles Place, and that the family Bible entry may reflect the place where the family was based, rather than the place of birth.

I have transcribed the relevant directory entries into the notebook:

The Archival Research Notebook notes that Lim Tian Soo birth_place was Raffles Place. Record status: historical.

- 1880: "Lim Cheng Huat, trader, 12 Raffles Place"
- 1885: "Lim Cheng Huat, trader, 12 Raffles Place"
- 1890: "Lim Tian Soo, clerk, 7 Raffles Place"

I should note that the directories are published annually, but the entries are based on information collected the previous year. So the 1880 directory reflects information from 1879. This means that Lim Cheng Huat was at Raffles Place by 1879 at the latest.

The directories are not as reliable as the birth register, but they are useful for establishing residence patterns. They are compiled from self-reported information, and they may contain errors in spelling or address. However, the consistency across three editions is suggestive.

---

**23 March 1990**

I wrote to the Registry of Births and Deaths in Malacca, as suggested by Arkib Negara Malaysia. I requested a search of the 1875 birth register for entry no. 412, and I enclosed a copy of the index entry. I also asked whether the register for 1875 has any marginal annotations or corrections that might not be visible on the microfilm.

I have not received a reply yet. I will wait a few weeks before following up.

Meanwhile, I have been thinking about the old street directories again. The 1880 directory is the earliest one that I have found that lists Lim Cheng Huat. But I should check the 1870s directories as well. The library has a run of directories from 1870 to 1900, but they are on microfilm and the earlier years are in poor condition. I will try to look at them next week.

---
I have been looking at the 1870s street directories on microfilm. The image quality is very poor, and the film is scratched. I have managed to read the following entries:

- 1872: "Lim Cheng Huat, trader, 7 Raffles Place"
- 1875: "Lim Cheng Huat, trader, 12 Raffles Place"
- 1878: "Lim Cheng Huat, trader, 12 Raffles Place"

This shows that Lim Cheng Huat was at Raffles Place from at least 1872. The earlier entries are for 7 Raffles Place, and the later entries are for 12 Raffles Place. The change of address may indicate a move to larger premises, or it may simply reflect a renumbering of the street.

I have transcribed these entries into the notebook.

The directories are not as reliable as the birth register, but they are useful for establishing residence patterns. They are compiled from self-reported information, and they may contain errors in spelling or address. However, the consistency across five editions is suggestive.

---

**30 April 1990**

I have received a letter from Swan & Maclaren. They confirm that the firm was responsible for the design of the house at Nassim Road, but they do not have the original plans. Their records from that period were destroyed during the Japanese occupation. However, they have a copy of a photograph of the house, taken shortly after completion. The photograph shows a two-storey building with a wide verandah and a tiled roof. I have asked for a copy of the photograph, and they have agreed to send one.

The letter also mentions that the contractor was "Messrs. Howarth & Co." I have not come across this name before. I will look for references to the contractor in the newspapers.

---

**7 May 1990**

I have found a reference to the contractor in the *Straits Times* of 3 December 1901, page 4: "Messrs. Howarth & Co. have completed the contract for the residence of Mr. Lim Cheng Huat at Nassim Road. The work has been carried out to the satisfaction of the architect, and the keys have been handed over to the owner."

This suggests that the house was completed by the end of 1901. The exact date of completion is not given, but the article implies that the work was finished.

I have also been trying to establish the construction year of the Lim Family Mansion. According to the Archival Research Notebook, Lim Family Mansion construction_year was 1901. Record status: historical. This is consistent with the newspaper articles and the Municipal Council minutes. The house was therefore built in 1901, and it was completed by the end of that year.

I should note that the construction year is distinct from the year in which the land was acquired. I have not yet found the deed for the purchase of the land. The land at Nassim Road was part of a larger estate, and it may have been acquired several years before the house was built. I will need to look at the land records.

---

**14 May 1990**

I have been looking at the land records at the Singapore Land Office. The records for the early 1900s are held at the National Archives, and they are indexed by lot number. I have found a reference to Lot 42, Nassim Road, in the register of titles for 1900. The register shows that the land was transferred to Lim Cheng Huat on 15 November 1900. The previous owner was "Raffles Institution," which held the land as part of its endowment.

This is an important finding. It shows that Lim Cheng Huat acquired the land in November 1900, and that the house was built the following year. The construction year of 1901 is therefore consistent with the land purchase.

I have made a copy of the register entry and placed it in the file.

---

**21 May 1990**

I have received the photograph from Swan & Maclaren. It is a sepia-toned print, approximately 15 cm by 20 cm, mounted on a card. The photograph shows the front elevation of the house. The building is two storeys, with a central portico and a verandah on both levels. The roof is tiled, and there is a chimney at the rear. The garden is not yet planted, and there is a wooden fence along the road.
**Archival Research Notebook**

**28 May 1990**

I have been thinking about the photograph from Swan & Maclaren. The print itself is in good condition, but the mounting card has a pencil note on the back, written in a different hand from the one that signed the photographer's stamp. The note reads: "No. 12, taken for Mrs. Lim, 1902." This is puzzling because the house was completed in 1901, and the garden in the photograph is bare. Perhaps the photograph was taken shortly after completion, and the note refers to a later printing or a different negative. I will not rely on the note for dating.

I have also started to compare the photograph with the description given in the *Straits Times* article of 10 January 1902. The article describes the verandah as "spacious" and the portico as "commanding." The photograph supports this. The chimney at the rear is visible, which the article does not mention. I should note that the article was probably written before the garden was planted, which is consistent with the bare garden in the photograph.

---

**4 June 1990**

I have been attempting to trace the Lim family's connection to the land before 1900. The register of titles shows that Raffles Institution held the land as part of its endowment, but I have not found the original grant. I have consulted the *Proceedings of the Straits Settlements Legislative Council* for the 1880s, but there is no mention of the Nassim Road land. The land may have been part of a larger grant to the Institution, and I will need to look at the early maps.

I have also been looking at the 1893 street directory. It does not list Nassim Road, which suggests that the road was not yet built or was not yet named. The 1898 directory lists the road, but with no houses. This is consistent with the land being vacant until the Lims acquired it.

---

**11 June 1990**

I have received a reply from the National Archives regarding my query about the Lim Family Mansion photographs. The Archives holds a collection of photographs from the estate of a later owner, and there is one photograph of the house from the 1920s. The photograph shows the house with a mature garden, and there is a car parked in the drive. I have requested a copy.

The Archives also holds a plan of the house, dated 1925, which shows a number of alterations. The plan shows that a service wing was added to the rear, and that the portico was widened. This is useful for understanding the later history of the house, but it does not bear on the construction year.

---

**18 June 1990**

I have been trying to verify a family story about the Lims. According to a letter written by Lim Cheng Huat's daughter, the family kept a pair of stone lions at the entrance to the mansion. The letter, which is in the possession of a descendant, states that the lions were brought from China in 1902. I have not been able to verify this from any other source. The 1925 plan does not show the lions, but the plan may not have included the garden details. I will note this as unverified.

I have also been looking at the probate records for Lim Cheng Huat. He died in 1918, and his estate was administered by the court. The probate file includes an inventory of the household effects, but it does not mention the lions. The inventory does mention "2 stone ornaments" in the garden, which may or may not be the lions. This is inconclusive.

---

**25 June 1990**

I have spent the morning at the National Archives, looking at the land records for the adjacent lots. The Lim property at Lot 42 is bordered by Lot 41 to the west and Lot 43 to the east. Lot 41 was owned by a European merchant, and Lot 43 was owned by a Chinese association. I have not found any indication that the Lims acquired either adjoining lot.

I have also been looking at the road records. Nassim Road was constructed in 1899, and the road reserve was 60 feet. The road was macadamized, and there was a footpath on one side. The records do not mention the Lims, but they confirm that the road existed before the house was built.
**Archival Research Notebook**
**Tan Chye Hin**
**Vol. 2, Entries 1990–2016**

---

**2 July 1990**

I have received a reply from the Public Works Department regarding the construction records for the Lim mansion at Lot 42 Nassim Road. The PWD file (PWD/Singapore/1899/1187) contains the original application for a building permit, dated 14 March 1899, and the certificate of occupation, dated 12 September 1899. The permit was issued to Lim Cheng Huat, described in the file as "merchant, of Boat Quay." This confirms the construction year of 1899, which I had previously inferred from the road records and the 1925 plan.

The PWD file also includes a specification sheet, which lists the materials used. The walls were of brick, plastered and painted. The roof was of clay tiles, and the floors were of timber. There is no mention of the stone lions in this file either. I will regard the lions as unverified, and I will note this in my summary for the family.

The file contains a note, dated 17 August 1899, from the Municipal Engineer, stating that the building was "completed in accordance with the approved plans, with the exception of the portico, which has been widened by two feet." This is interesting. The 1925 plan shows the portico as widened, but the widening may have been done at the time of construction, not later. I will need to compare the 1899 plans with the 1925 plans more carefully.

---

**9 July 1990**

I have located a descendant of the Lim family, a Mrs. Grace Tan (née Lim), who lives in Kuala Lumpur. Her mother was a daughter of Lim Cheng Huat. Mrs. Tan has agreed to speak with me, and she has several family documents that she is willing to share. I have written to her, care of her address in Bangsar, and I have enclosed a list of questions.

The questions I have asked are:

1. The date of Lim Cheng Huat's arrival in Singapore from China.
2. The name of his first wife, and the date of their marriage.
3. The names and birth dates of all his children.
4. Whether the family kept any records of the construction of the house at Nassim Road.
5. The fate of the stone lions, if she knows of them.
6. Whether there are any photographs of the house from before 1920.

I have also asked whether she knows of any letters or diaries written by Lim Cheng Huat himself. I am particularly interested in any correspondence that might mention the house or the family's business affairs.

---

**16 July 1990**

I have received a letter from Mrs. Grace Tan. She writes that her mother, Lim Siew Lan, was born in 1908, the youngest of seven children. Mrs. Tan does not have any documents from her grandfather's time, but she remembers her mother speaking of a pair of stone lions at the entrance to the house. According to Mrs. Tan, the lions were removed during the Japanese occupation, when the house was requisitioned by the military. She does not know what became of them.

This is a plausible account, but it is not corroborated by any written source. The probate inventory of 1918 mentions "2 stone ornaments" in the garden, which I have noted before. The family story is that the lions were brought from China in 1902, but I have no independent evidence of this. I will record this as a family tradition, not as a verified fact.

Mrs. Tan has also provided the names and birth dates of Lim Cheng Huat's children:

1. Lim Cheng Huat, son, b. 1880 (died in infancy)
2. Lim Siew Kim, daughter, b. 1882
3. Lim Cheng Guan, son, b. 1885
4. Lim Cheng Keat, son, b. 1888
5. Lim Siew Lan, daughter, b. 1908

The gap between 1888 and 1908 is notable. It is possible that there were other children who died in infancy, or that the family had difficulty conceiving. I will ask Mrs. Tan about this in my next letter.

---

**23 July 1990**

I have spent the day at the Registry of Births and Deaths, looking for the birth records of Lim Cheng Huat's children. I have found the following:

- Lim Siew Kim, born 12 February 1882, father: Lim Cheng Huat, mother: Chua Neo.
- Lim Cheng Guan, born 3 June 1885, father: Lim Cheng Huat, mother: Chua Neo.
- Lim Cheng Keat, born 19 November 1888, father: Lim Cheng Huat, mother: Chua Neo.
- Lim Siew Lan, born 4 March 1908, father: Lim Cheng Huat, mother: Chua Neo.

**Entry 002 — 5 February 1985, 2:30 pm**
Regular meeting. Present: Mrs. Wong, Mr. Tan, Mr. Goh. Mr. Lim sent apologies.

documents.title: Archival Research Notebook
documents.content:
Spent the morning at the National Archives of Singapore (NAS) on Canning Rise. I was looking for the Straits Settlements Birth Registers, but I got distracted by the index to the Malacca Registration District. The index is on microfilm (NAS MICROFILM 6789, reel 2). I found an entry that could be relevant:

- Name: Lim Tian Soo (also spelled “Lim Tian Su” in the index)
- Registration District: Malacca
- Year: 1875
- Volume: 4, Folio: 118

I did not pull the actual register page because the microfilm reader was having focus issues. The index entry is promising but I must see the original page to verify the date of birth and the parents’ names. The index alone is not sufficient for a genealogical citation.

---

**22 January 1990**

Wrote to the National Archives of Malaysia (Arkib Negara Malaysia), Kuala Lumpur, to ask if they hold the Malacca Birth Registers for 1875. I have a standard request letter that I use for such queries. I sent it by registered post. I should expect a response in 4–6 weeks.

Also telephoned Cousin Margaret to ask if she has any other letters from Auntie Siew that mention Uncle Tian. She said she has a small tin box of papers that belonged to her mother (my mother’s other sister, Siew Hiang). She will look through it when she has time. I reminded her that even a scrap of paper with a date would help.

---

**3 February 1990**

Cousin Margaret telephoned. She found a postcard from Auntie Siew to her mother, postmarked 1935, that mentions “Tian Soo’s eldest daughter is getting married in June.” This is not a birth record, but it confirms that Lim Tian Soo had at least one daughter. The family tree in my possession (hand-drawn by my grandfather, circa 1950) lists a daughter named Lim Poh Neo, but gives no dates. I will add a marginal note to the family tree: “Poh Neo, daughter of Tian Soo, married June 1935 (per postcard, Siew to Siew Hiang, 1935).”

Marginalia on the postcard: The postmark is partially illegible, but the year 1935 is clear. The card was posted from Malacca, and the stamp is the 2-cent Straits Settlements issue with a portrait of King George V.

---

In the Archival Research Notebook, Lim Tian Soo birth_year is recorded as 1875. Record status: historical.

**17 February 1990**

Received a reply from Arkib Negara Malaysia. They confirm that they hold the Malacca Birth Registers for the period 1872–1900, but the registers for 1875 are in poor condition. They suggest I write to the Registry of Births and Deaths, Malacca, to request a search. They also note that some registers were damaged during the war, and that the microfilm copies held in Singapore may be the best source.

I have decided to try the Singapore microfilm again, but this time I will use a different reader. The NAS staff said that the focus issue is on the machine, not the film. I will book the machine for a full morning session.

---

**24 February 1990**

Morning at NAS. I booked microfilm reader 3, which is in better condition. I re-loaded reel 2 of MICROFILM 6789 and went to the Malacca Birth Register for 1875. The index entry led me to Volume 4, Folio 118. The page is very faint, but I could make out the following:

- No. of entry: 412
- Name of child: Lim Tian Soo
- Sex: Male
- Date of birth: 17 March 1875
- Place of birth: 8, Jalan Tengkera, Malacca
- Name of father: Lim Cheng Huat (occupation: trader)
- Name of mother: Tan Kim Neo (no occupation listed)
- Informant: Lim Cheng Huat (father), 21 March 1875

This is the registration record. The date of birth is 17 March 1875. The index had only given the year, so this is a new finding. I have transcribed the entry fully into the notebook. I have also made a photocopy of the page (NAS photocopy request no. 1990-0214). I will file the photocopy with the family papers.

I must be careful: the register is a contemporary record, made in 1875, and is therefore a historical source. The birth year of Lim Tian Soo is 1875. This is now a recorded fact in this notebook, based on the register entry. I will not revise this unless I find a conflicting record, which is unlikely because the register is the primary source.

---

**2 March 1990**

documents.title: Archival Research Notebook
documents.content:
I have been thinking about the place of birth. The register says "8, Jalan Tengkera, Malacca." This is a street address. But the family story, as told by my grandmother and recorded in the family Bible, says that Lim Tian Soo was born at Raffles Place. I have never been able to reconcile these two statements. The family Bible entry is in my aunt's handwriting, and she wrote it down in the 1930s, many years after the event. It says: "Lim Tian Soo, born at Raffles Place, in the year 1875." No month or day is given.

I need to be careful here. The register is a contemporary record, made in 1875, and is therefore a historical source. The family Bible is a later record, made in the 1930s, and is therefore not contemporary. However, the family Bible may preserve an oral tradition that is older than the written entry. The question is whether the oral tradition is reliable.

I have decided to investigate the Raffles Place connection further. There are several possibilities:

1. The family moved from Malacca to Singapore when Lim Tian Soo was an infant, and the family Bible entry reflects the place where he grew up, not where he was born.
2. The family had a business address at Raffles Place, and the Bible entry confuses the family residence with the business premises.
3. The Bible entry is simply wrong.

I will need to find evidence that bears on these possibilities. The first step is to establish whether the family had any connection to Raffles Place in the 1870s or 1880s.

---

**16 March 1990**

Spent the afternoon at the National Library, looking at old street directories. I consulted the Singapore and Straits Directory for 1880, 1885, and 1890. These are available on microfilm at the library. The 1880 directory lists a "Lim Cheng Huat, trader" at 12 Raffles Place. The 1885 directory lists the same name at the same address. The 1890 directory does not list Lim Cheng Huat, but it does list a "Lim Tian Soo, clerk" at 7 Raffles Place.

This is a significant finding. The father, Lim Cheng Huat, was at Raffles Place by 1880, which is only five years after the birth of Lim Tian Soo. The son, Lim Tian Soo, is listed at Raffles Place in 1890, when he would have been fifteen years old. This suggests that the family had a long association with Raffles Place, and that the family Bible entry may reflect the place where the family was based, rather than the place of birth.

I have transcribed the relevant directory entries into the notebook:

The Archival Research Notebook notes that Lim Tian Soo birth_place was Raffles Place. Record status: historical.

- 1880: "Lim Cheng Huat, trader, 12 Raffles Place"
- 1885: "Lim Cheng Huat, trader, 12 Raffles Place"
- 1890: "Lim Tian Soo, clerk, 7 Raffles Place"

I should note that the directories are published annually, but the entries are based on information collected the previous year. So the 1880 directory reflects information from 1879. This means that Lim Cheng Huat was at Raffles Place by 1879 at the latest.

The directories are not as reliable as the birth register, but they are useful for establishing residence patterns. They are compiled from self-reported information, and they may contain errors in spelling or address. However, the consistency across three editions is suggestive.

---

**23 March 1990**

I wrote to the Registry of Births and Deaths in Malacca, as suggested by Arkib Negara Malaysia. I requested a search of the 1875 birth register for entry no. 412, and I enclosed a copy of the index entry. I also asked whether the register for 1875 has any marginal annotations or corrections that might not be visible on the microfilm.

I have not received a reply yet. I will wait a few weeks before following up.

Meanwhile, I have been thinking about the old street directories again. The 1880 directory is the earliest one that I have found that lists Lim Cheng Huat. But I should check the 1870s directories as well. The library has a run of directories from 1870 to 1900, but they are on microfilm and the earlier years are in poor condition. I will try to look at them next week.

---

documents.title: Archival Research Notebook
documents.content:
I have been looking at the 1870s street directories on microfilm. The image quality is very poor, and the film is scratched. I have managed to read the following entries:

- 1872: "Lim Cheng Huat, trader, 7 Raffles Place"
- 1875: "Lim Cheng Huat, trader, 12 Raffles Place"
- 1878: "Lim Cheng Huat, trader, 12 Raffles Place"

This shows that Lim Cheng Huat was at Raffles Place from at least 1872. The earlier entries are for 7 Raffles Place, and the later entries are for 12 Raffles Place. The change of address may indicate a move to larger premises, or it may simply reflect a renumbering of the street.

I have transcribed these entries into the notebook.

The directories are not as reliable as the birth register, but they are useful for establishing residence patterns. They are compiled from self-reported information, and they may contain errors in spelling or address. However, the consistency across five editions is suggestive.

---

**30 April 1990**

I have received a letter from Swan & Maclaren. They confirm that the firm was responsible for the design of the house at Nassim Road, but they do not have the original plans. Their records from that period were destroyed during the Japanese occupation. However, they have a copy of a photograph of the house, taken shortly after completion. The photograph shows a two-storey building with a wide verandah and a tiled roof. I have asked for a copy of the photograph, and they have agreed to send one.

The letter also mentions that the contractor was "Messrs. Howarth & Co." I have not come across this name before. I will look for references to the contractor in the newspapers.

---

**7 May 1990**

I have found a reference to the contractor in the *Straits Times* of 3 December 1901, page 4: "Messrs. Howarth & Co. have completed the contract for the residence of Mr. Lim Cheng Huat at Nassim Road. The work has been carried out to the satisfaction of the architect, and the keys have been handed over to the owner."

This suggests that the house was completed by the end of 1901. The exact date of completion is not given, but the article implies that the work was finished.

I have also been trying to establish the construction year of the Lim Family Mansion. According to the Archival Research Notebook, Lim Family Mansion construction_year was 1901. Record status: historical. This is consistent with the newspaper articles and the Municipal Council minutes. The house was therefore built in 1901, and it was completed by the end of that year.

I should note that the construction year is distinct from the year in which the land was acquired. I have not yet found the deed for the purchase of the land. The land at Nassim Road was part of a larger estate, and it may have been acquired several years before the house was built. I will need to look at the land records.

---

**14 May 1990**

I have been looking at the land records at the Singapore Land Office. The records for the early 1900s are held at the National Archives, and they are indexed by lot number. I have found a reference to Lot 42, Nassim Road, in the register of titles for 1900. The register shows that the land was transferred to Lim Cheng Huat on 15 November 1900. The previous owner was "Raffles Institution," which held the land as part of its endowment.

This is an important finding. It shows that Lim Cheng Huat acquired the land in November 1900, and that the house was built the following year. The construction year of 1901 is therefore consistent with the land purchase.

I have made a copy of the register entry and placed it in the file.

---

**21 May 1990**

I have received the photograph from Swan & Maclaren. It is a sepia-toned print, approximately 15 cm by 20 cm, mounted on a card. The photograph shows the front elevation of the house. The building is two storeys, with a central portico and a verandah on both levels. The roof is tiled, and there is a chimney at the rear. The garden is not yet planted, and there is a wooden fence along the road.

**28 May 1990**

I have been thinking about the photograph from Swan & Maclaren. The print itself is in good condition, but the mounting card has a pencil note on the back, written in a different hand from the one that signed the photographer's stamp. The note reads: "No. 12, taken for Mrs. Lim, 1902." This is puzzling because the house was completed in 1901, and the garden in the photograph is bare. Perhaps the photograph was taken shortly after completion, and the note refers to a later printing or a different negative. I will not rely on the note for dating.

I have also started to compare the photograph with the description given in the *Straits Times* article of 10 January 1902. The article describes the verandah as "spacious" and the portico as "commanding." The photograph supports this. The chimney at the rear is visible, which the article does not mention. I should note that the article was probably written before the garden was planted, which is consistent with the bare garden in the photograph.

---

**4 June 1990**

I have been attempting to trace the Lim family's connection to the land before 1900. The register of titles shows that Raffles Institution held the land as part of its endowment, but I have not found the original grant. I have consulted the *Proceedings of the Straits Settlements Legislative Council* for the 1880s, but there is no mention of the Nassim Road land. The land may have been part of a larger grant to the Institution, and I will need to look at the early maps.

I have also been looking at the 1893 street directory. It does not list Nassim Road, which suggests that the road was not yet built or was not yet named. The 1898 directory lists the road, but with no houses. This is consistent with the land being vacant until the Lims acquired it.

---

**11 June 1990**

I have received a reply from the National Archives regarding my query about the Lim Family Mansion photographs. The Archives holds a collection of photographs from the estate of a later owner, and there is one photograph of the house from the 1920s. The photograph shows the house with a mature garden, and there is a car parked in the drive. I have requested a copy.

The Archives also holds a plan of the house, dated 1925, which shows a number of alterations. The plan shows that a service wing was added to the rear, and that the portico was widened. This is useful for understanding the later history of the house, but it does not bear on the construction year.

---

**18 June 1990**

I have been trying to verify a family story about the Lims. According to a letter written by Lim Cheng Huat's daughter, the family kept a pair of stone lions at the entrance to the mansion. The letter, which is in the possession of a descendant, states that the lions were brought from China in 1902. I have not been able to verify this from any other source. The 1925 plan does not show the lions, but the plan may not have included the garden details. I will note this as unverified.

I have also been looking at the probate records for Lim Cheng Huat. He died in 1918, and his estate was administered by the court. The probate file includes an inventory of the household effects, but it does not mention the lions. The inventory does mention "2 stone ornaments" in the garden, which may or may not be the lions. This is inconclusive.

---

**25 June 1990**

I have spent the morning at the National Archives, looking at the land records for the adjacent lots. The Lim property at Lot 42 is bordered by Lot 41 to the west and Lot 43 to the east. Lot 41 was owned by a European merchant, and Lot 43 was owned by a Chinese association. I have not found any indication that the Lims acquired either adjoining lot.

I have also been looking at the road records. Nassim Road was constructed in 1899, and the road reserve was 60 feet. The road was macadamized, and there was a footpath on one side. The records do not mention the Lims, but they confirm that the road existed before the house was built.

documents.title: Archival Research Notebook
documents.content:
**Archival Research Notebook**
**Tan Chye Hin**
**Vol. 2, Entries 1990–2016**

---

**2 July 1990**

I have received a reply from the Public Works Department regarding the construction records for the Lim mansion at Lot 42 Nassim Road. The PWD file (PWD/Singapore/1899/1187) contains the original application for a building permit, dated 14 March 1899, and the certificate of occupation, dated 12 September 1899. The permit was issued to Lim Cheng Huat, described in the file as "merchant, of Boat Quay." This confirms the construction year of 1899, which I had previously inferred from the road records and the 1925 plan.

The PWD file also includes a specification sheet, which lists the materials used. The walls were of brick, plastered and painted. The roof was of clay tiles, and the floors were of timber. There is no mention of the stone lions in this file either. I will regard the lions as unverified, and I will note this in my summary for the family.

The file contains a note, dated 17 August 1899, from the Municipal Engineer, stating that the building was "completed in accordance with the approved plans, with the exception of the portico, which has been widened by two feet." This is interesting. The 1925 plan shows the portico as widened, but the widening may have been done at the time of construction, not later. I will need to compare the 1899 plans with the 1925 plans more carefully.

---

**9 July 1990**

I have located a descendant of the Lim family, a Mrs. Grace Tan (née Lim), who lives in Kuala Lumpur. Her mother was a daughter of Lim Cheng Huat. Mrs. Tan has agreed to speak with me, and she has several family documents that she is willing to share. I have written to her, care of her address in Bangsar, and I have enclosed a list of questions.

The questions I have asked are:

1. The date of Lim Cheng Huat's arrival in Singapore from China.
2. The name of his first wife, and the date of their marriage.
3. The names and birth dates of all his children.
4. Whether the family kept any records of the construction of the house at Nassim Road.
5. The fate of the stone lions, if she knows of them.
6. Whether there are any photographs of the house from before 1920.

I have also asked whether she knows of any letters or diaries written by Lim Cheng Huat himself. I am particularly interested in any correspondence that might mention the house or the family's business affairs.

---

**16 July 1990**

I have received a letter from Mrs. Grace Tan. She writes that her mother, Lim Siew Lan, was born in 1908, the youngest of seven children. Mrs. Tan does not have any documents from her grandfather's time, but she remembers her mother speaking of a pair of stone lions at the entrance to the house. According to Mrs. Tan, the lions were removed during the Japanese occupation, when the house was requisitioned by the military. She does not know what became of them.

This is a plausible account, but it is not corroborated by any written source. The probate inventory of 1918 mentions "2 stone ornaments" in the garden, which I have noted before. The family story is that the lions were brought from China in 1902, but I have no independent evidence of this. I will record this as a family tradition, not as a verified fact.

Mrs. Tan has also provided the names and birth dates of Lim Cheng Huat's children:

1. Lim Cheng Huat, son, b. 1880 (died in infancy)
2. Lim Siew Kim, daughter, b. 1882
3. Lim Cheng Guan, son, b. 1885
4. Lim Cheng Keat, son, b. 1888
5. Lim Siew Lan, daughter, b. 1908

The gap between 1888 and 1908 is notable. It is possible that there were other children who died in infancy, or that the family had difficulty conceiving. I will ask Mrs. Tan about this in my next letter.

---

**23 July 1990**

I have spent the day at the Registry of Births and Deaths, looking for the birth records of Lim Cheng Huat's children. I have found the following:

- Lim Siew Kim, born 12 February 1882, father: Lim Cheng Huat, mother: Chua Neo.
- Lim Cheng Guan, born 3 June 1885, father: Lim Cheng Huat, mother: Chua Neo.
- Lim Cheng Keat, born 19 November 1888, father: Lim Cheng Huat, mother: Chua Neo.
- Lim Siew Lan, born 4 March 1908, father: Lim Cheng Huat, mother: Chua Neo.

**EDITORIAL COMMITTEE MEETING MINUTES**

**Meeting No.:** 12/2016
**Date:** 14 November 2016, Monday
**Time:** 2:30 pm – 4:45 pm
**Venue:** Meeting Room 3, Level 2, Singapore Heritage Society Office, 22B Waterloo Street
**Chairperson:** Mr. Goh Kiat Seng
**Secretary:** Ms. Wong Mei Ling

**Attendees:**
Mr. Goh Kiat Seng (Chairperson)
Mr. Tan Chye Hin
Mr. David Ng
Ms. Faridah Bte Ahmad
Ms. Lim Siew Hong (by invitation, item 4 only)
Mr. Rajendran s/o Muthusamy
Ms. Chan Wai Han

**Absent with Apologies:**
Mr. Lee Chee Meng
Dr. Norazlina Bte Hassan

**1. Minutes of the Previous Meeting**

The minutes of the previous meeting held on 10 October 2016 were circulated to members by email on 15 October 2016. The minutes were confirmed as a true and accurate record of the proceedings, subject to one correction: in item 4.2, the name of the photographer of the 1957 wedding photograph should read "Mr. Lim Cheng Huat" and not "Mr. Lim Cheng Watt". The correction was noted by the Secretary. The minutes were then approved and signed by the Chairperson.

**2. Matters Arising**

2.1 *Access to Lim Ancestral Association Records (Item 3.6, Meeting 3/2010)* – Mr. Tan Chye Hin reported that the conditions attached to the Association’s approval, as noted in the minutes of the meeting held on 19 April 2010, had been complied with. The Association had been provided with a draft of Chapter 4 of the manuscript for its review. No objections had been received. The Association’s management committee had, however, requested that the committee acknowledge the Association’s assistance in the publication’s acknowledgements page. The committee agreed to this request.

2.2 *Oral History Interviews (Item 5.2, Meeting 8/2016)* – Ms. Faridah Bte Ahmad confirmed that the transcripts of the three interviews conducted in August and September 2016 had been reviewed by the interviewees. Two signed release forms had been returned. The third, from Mr. Lim Boon Keng, had not yet been received. Ms. Faridah agreed to follow up with Mr. Lim by the end of November.

2.3 *Photographs from Ms. Lim Siew Hong (Item 6.1, Meeting 10/2016)* – Ms. Lim Siew Hong had delivered a total of 47 photographs to the Society’s office on 2 November 2016. Mr. Tan Chye Hin had scanned all 47 images at 600 dpi. The original photographs were returned to Ms. Lim on 7 November 2016. A receipt acknowledging the return was signed by Ms. Lim and retained by the Secretary.

**3. Manuscript Status Report**

3.1 Mr. Tan Chye Hin reported that the full manuscript, comprising 12 chapters, an introduction, and a conclusion, had been completed. The total word count was approximately 86,000 words. The manuscript had been circulated to the committee on 28 October 2016.

3.2 The committee had been requested to submit their comments and corrections to Mr. Tan by 11 November 2016. As of the date of this meeting, comments had been received from Mr. David Ng, Ms. Chan Wai Han, and Ms. Faridah Bte Ahmad. Mr. Rajendran had indicated that his comments would be submitted by the end of this week. No comments had been received from Mr. Lee Chee Meng or Dr. Norazlina Bte Hassan.

3.3 Mr. Tan reported that the comments received to date were largely editorial in nature. A small number of factual points had been raised, and Mr. Tan had verified these against his research notes. He confirmed that the factual points raised by Ms. Chan Wai Han in relation to the genealogy chart in Chapter 2 were correct, and that the chart would be amended accordingly.

3.4 The Chairperson noted that the publication schedule was tight. The printer had been booked for the first week of January 2017. It was therefore essential that the final manuscript be submitted to the designer by 5 December 2016 at the latest.

**4. Design and Production**

4.1 Ms. Lim Siew Hong, who had been invited to attend this item, reported on the design proposals she had prepared. She presented two cover design concepts to the committee. The first concept used a sepia-toned photograph of the Lim family home at 12 Upper Cross Street, taken circa 1935, as the central image. The second concept used a more abstract design, incorporating a stylised family tree motif.
